populations.name: Neandertals
populations.description: An archaic human group of western Eurasia, known from fossils and from several high-quality genomes. Their DNA survives in all present-day people whose ancestry lies largely outside Africa.
populations.genetic_profile: Sampled genomes range from the Altai Mountains to western Europe. The Neandertals who contributed DNA to modern humans were closer to the western (Vindija, Mezmaiskaya) Neandertals than to the Altai individual.

membership.notes: AADR labels ending in _Neanderthal. Excludes the Neandertal–Denisovan first-generation offspring (Russia_Denisova_Neanderthal_Mix).

caveats: Most sampled Neandertal genomes predate the V1 window; only a few late individuals (about 50,000–40,000 years ago) fall inside it.

populations.name: Denisovans
populations.description: An archaic human group known mainly from genomes recovered at Denisova Cave in the Altai. Denisovan-related DNA survives at the highest levels in people of Oceania and parts of Island Southeast Asia.
populations.genetic_profile: Related to Neandertals. The Denisovans who contributed DNA to modern humans were only distantly related to the sampled Altai individual; at least two differently related Denisovan sources are detected in present-day East Asians.

region.name: Known from the Altai (Denisova Cave); inferred elsewhere in Asia

membership.notes: Only the genetically Denisovan individuals. Russia_DenisovaCave (a ~24,000-year-old modern human from the same cave) is deliberately excluded.

caveats: All sampled Denisovan genomes predate the V1 window; the populations that admixed with modern humans are unsampled and their locations unknown.
AADR also has a modern human from Denisova Cave; a site is not a population.

populations.name: Shared ancestors of non-Africans (inferred)
populations.description: A modelled population: the common ancestors of nearly all present-day people whose ancestry lies largely outside Africa, who received Neandertal gene flow before dispersing. No individual from it has been sampled and its location is unknown.

membership.notes: Inferred only.

caveats: The time range shown is the window of the shared Neandertal gene flow (50,500–43,500 years ago, Iasi et al. 2024), not the population's lifespan.

populations.name: Zlatý kůň/Ranis population
populations.description: A small population of early modern humans known from two sites in central Europe, about 45,000 years ago. The individuals were closely related to each other, even across sites.
populations.genetic_profile: The earliest split from the out-of-Africa population sampled so far. No detectable continuity with later Europeans.
populations.archaeological_context: The Ranis remains are associated with the Lincombian–Ranisian–Jerzmanowician (LRJ) assemblage.

membership.notes: All Ranis and Zlatý kůň individuals.

populations.name: Bacho Kiro IUP-associated individuals
populations.description: Individuals from Bacho Kiro Cave in Bulgaria, about 46,000–43,000 years ago, buried with an Initial Upper Palaeolithic stone-tool assemblage. All had Neandertal ancestors only a few generations back.
populations.genetic_profile: More closely related to later East Asians and Native Americans than to later western Eurasians.

membership.notes: IUP layers only; the later Bacho Kiro UP individual is not included.

populations.name: Ust'-Ishim individual
populations.description: A single man who lived about 45,000 years ago in western Siberia. His genome comes from a population that lived before, or around the time of, the separation of western and eastern Eurasian populations.

membership.notes: One individual.

caveats: A single individual: a population of one is a placeholder for an otherwise unsampled group.

populations.name: Oase 1
populations.description: An early modern human from Peştera cu Oase, Romania, about 40,000 years ago, with a Neandertal ancestor only four to six generations back.

membership.notes: AADR labels Oase 1 as Romania_IUP.

caveats: A single individual.
AADR flags this individual's data as CRITICAL (quality/contamination warning); it is shown with that warning because it is the subject of the cited study.

populations.name: Tianyuan individual
populations.description: A man who lived about 40,000 years ago near present-day Beijing, more closely related to Asians than to Europeans but with an unexpected link to a 35,000-year-old individual from Belgium.

membership.notes: One individual.

caveats: A single individual.

populations.name: Early European founder population (Kostenki/Sunghir-related)
populations.description: Individuals from western Russia, about 38,000–32,000 years ago, who belong to the founder population that contributed to all later sampled European hunter-gatherers until about 14,000 years ago.

membership.notes: Kostenki 14 is the type individual in Fu 2016; Sunghir is grouped with it as related to the Věstonice cluster in Posth 2023.

caveats: Grouping Kostenki and Sunghir together is our simplification; both papers treat them as related members of the early European founder lineage.

populations.name: Goyet Q116-1-related individuals (Aurignacian-associated)
populations.description: Individuals from Goyet Cave in Belgium, about 35,000 years ago, associated with the Aurignacian. Their ancestry reappears later in western European groups.

membership.notes: Goyet Q116-1 and Q376-3.

caveats: Two individuals.

populations.name: Věstonice cluster (Gravettian-associated, central and southern Europe)
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers buried with Gravettian material in central and southern Europe, about 34,000–26,000 years ago, who share a genetic profile distinct from that of Gravettian-associated people further west.
populations.archaeological_context: Gravettian. The same archaeological culture is associated with two genetic profiles (see Fournol cluster).

membership.notes: Sites named by Posth 2023: Dolní Věstonice, Pavlov, Krems-Wachtberg, Paglicci, Ostuni.

caveats: The Gravettian-associated individuals from Goyet (Belgium) are assigned to this cluster by Fu 2016 but described as intermediate by Posth 2023; they are left unassigned here.

populations.name: Fournol cluster (Gravettian-associated, western Europe)
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers buried with Gravettian material in France and northeastern Iberia, about 31,000–26,000 years ago. Their ancestry resembles that of earlier Aurignacian-associated individuals from Belgium.

membership.notes: Sites named by Posth 2023: Ormesson, La Rochette, Fournol, Mollet III, Reclau Viver.

caveats: Few individuals.

populations.name: Ancient North Siberians (Yana)
populations.description: People who lived about 31,000 years ago at the Yana site in Arctic northeastern Siberia, distantly related to early western Eurasian hunter-gatherers.

membership.notes: Yana RHS individuals.

caveats: Two individuals.

populations.name: Ancient North Eurasians (Mal'ta, Afontova Gora)
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of south-central Siberia, about 24,000–17,000 years ago. Ancestry related to theirs later appears both in Native Americans and in western Eurasians.

membership.notes: MA-1 and Afontova Gora individuals.

caveats: Three individuals.

populations.name: Solutrean-associated individuals
populations.description: People buried with Solutrean material in Iberia and southern France during the Last Glacial Maximum, carrying ancestry related to the earlier Fournol cluster.
caveats: Very few individuals.

populations.name: Magdalenian-associated individuals (GoyetQ2 / El Mirón cluster)
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers buried with Magdalenian material, about 19,000–14,000 years ago, from Iberia to Poland. Their ancestry is modelled as mostly Fournol-related with a smaller Villabruna-related share.

membership.notes: Excludes the Late Magdalenian/Federmesser individuals at Oberkassel (WHG-like).

populations.name: Villabruna cluster (Epigravettian-associated)
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers associated with the Epigravettian in Italy, sampled from about 17,000 years ago. Their ancestry has links to the Near East and later spread across Europe.

populations.name: Western hunter-gatherers (WHG / Oberkassel cluster)
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of western and central Europe from about 14,000 years ago until farming, whose ancestry spread widely after the Last Glacial Maximum and later contributed to farming populations.

membership.notes: Late Glacial and Mesolithic hunter-gatherers west of the 'great divide'. Scandinavian, Baltic and Iron Gates hunter-gatherers, who carry mixed WHG/EHG ancestry, are not included.

caveats: Iberian hunter-gatherers show their own northwest–southeast substructure (Olalde 2019).

populations.name: Eastern hunter-gatherers (EHG / Sidelkino cluster)
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of the eastern European forest zone, about 11,000–7,000 years ago, with ancestry related both to western hunter-gatherers and to Ancient North Eurasians.

membership.notes: Karelia (Yuzhniy Oleniy Ostrov area) and Samara/Sidelkino individuals, the type groups for EHG.

populations.name: Caucasus hunter-gatherers (CHG)
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of western Georgia, about 13,300 and 9,700 years ago, who form a distinct ancient lineage. CHG-related ancestry later contributed to steppe populations.

membership.notes: Satsurblia and Kotias Klde. Older Georgian UP individuals (Dzudzuana, Kotias Klde UP) are not assigned.

caveats: Three individuals.

populations.name: Iberomaurusian-associated individuals (Taforalt)
populations.description: People buried at Taforalt cave in Morocco about 15,000 years ago, with Iberomaurusian material. Their ancestry links North Africa with the Near East and sub-Saharan Africa.
caveats: Claims verified against the abstract only.

populations.name: Natufian-associated hunter-gatherers
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of the southern Levant associated with the Natufian culture, before the beginning of farming. About half their ancestry is modelled as coming from a 'Basal Eurasian' lineage.
caveats: Few individuals.

populations.name: Anatolian Epipalaeolithic hunter-gatherer (Pınarbaşı)
populations.description: A hunter-gatherer from Pınarbaşı in central Anatolia, about 15,000 years ago, whose ancestry continues to a large degree in the region's first farmers.
caveats: A single individual.

populations.name: Basal Eurasian lineage (modelled)
populations.description: A modelled ancestral lineage that split from other non-African lineages before they diversified. It is needed to fit the ancestry of early Near Easterners and Early European Farmers, but no individual from it has been sampled.

membership.notes: Inferred only.

caveats: The time range is a display window only: the papers place the lineage's split before the diversification of other non-Africans and its contribution before the earliest sampled Natufians, without dating it precisely.

populations.name: Early farmers of the Zagros
populations.description: Early Neolithic people of the Zagros mountains in western Iran, among the earliest farmers, who descended largely from local hunter-gatherers and were genetically distinct from Anatolian and Levantine farmers.

populations.name: Early farmers of the southern Levant (PPNB)
populations.description: Pre-Pottery Neolithic farmers of Jordan and Israel, who descended largely from local Natufian-related hunter-gatherers.

populations.name: Early farmers of Anatolia
populations.description: Neolithic farmers of central and western Anatolia, whose ancestry continues largely from local hunter-gatherers and is closely related to that of the first farmers of Europe.

populations.name: Late Chalcolithic individuals of Peqi'in Cave
populations.description: People buried in Peqi'in Cave, northern Israel, during the Late Chalcolithic (about 4500–3900 BCE). They formed a homogeneous population modelled with Levantine, Iranian-related and Anatolian-related ancestry.
populations.archaeological_context: Late Chalcolithic of the southern Levant.

populations.name: Early farmers associated with Starčevo–Körös–Criș
populations.description: The first farming communities of southeastern Europe from the mid-7th millennium BCE, carrying ancestry mostly related to Anatolian farmers.
populations.archaeological_context: Starčevo, Körös and Criș complexes; Early Neolithic of Greece.

populations.name: LBK-associated farmers
populations.description: Farmers of the Linear Pottery (LBK) culture across central Europe, about 5500–4900 BCE, with mostly Anatolian-farmer-related ancestry and a small hunter-gatherer share.

populations.name: Early Neolithic farmers of Iberia
populations.description: Early farmers of the Iberian Peninsula, including Cardial-associated individuals, from the mid-6th millennium BCE.

populations.name: Neolithic farmers of Britain
populations.description: Farming communities of Britain from about 4000 BCE, whose ancestry derives mainly from continental farmers, with small, regionally varying contributions from local hunter-gatherers.

populations.name: Trypillia-associated farmers
populations.description: Farmers of the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture in present-day Ukraine and Moldova during the Eneolithic.

region.name: Forest-steppe north of the Black Sea

populations.name: Globular Amphora-associated individuals
populations.description: Late Neolithic people of central and eastern Europe associated with the Globular Amphora culture, about 3400–2800 BCE.

populations.name: Volga cline Eneolithic (Khvalynsk, Ekaterinovka)
populations.description: Eneolithic people of the middle Volga whose ancestry varies between Caucasus–Lower Volga-related and eastern hunter-gatherer-related ends of a cline.
caveats: Individuals on a cline are genetically heterogeneous by definition.

populations.name: Caucasus–Lower Volga cline Eneolithic (Berezhnovka)
populations.description: Eneolithic people of the lower Volga steppe at the northern end of a genetic cline rich in Caucasus hunter-gatherer-related ancestry. CLV-related ancestry later makes up most of Yamnaya ancestry.

membership.notes: Only the Berezhnovka individuals are clearly labelled in AADR v66.p1; other CLV-cline sites named by Lazaridis 2025 are not assigned yet.

caveats: Membership is incomplete: assigning the remaining CLV-cline individuals needs the paper's individual list.

populations.name: Serednii Stih-associated individuals (Dnipro cline)
populations.description: Eneolithic people of the Dnipro and Don steppe associated with the Serednii Stih culture, formed as Caucasus–Lower Volga-related people mixed with Ukraine Neolithic hunter-gatherers. Yamnaya ancestors formed from related groups.

populations.name: Maikop-associated individuals (North Caucasus)
populations.description: People of the North Caucasus associated with the Maikop culture in the 4th millennium BCE, genetically closer to populations south of the Caucasus than to their steppe neighbours.

membership.notes: Steppe Maikop individuals (with additional Siberian-related ancestry, Wang 2019) are not included.

populations.name: Yamnaya-associated individuals
populations.description: Herders buried in kurgans of the Yamnaya complex from about 3300 BCE, from Hungary to Kazakhstan. Genetically they are remarkably homogeneous, and ancestry related to theirs later spread widely across Europe and into Central Asia.
populations.genetic_profile: Combines Caucasus/Near Eastern-related and eastern European hunter-gatherer-related ancestry; competing models of how it formed are shown side by side.

populations.name: Corded Ware-associated individuals
populations.description: People buried with Corded Ware material across northern and central Europe from about 2900 BCE, most of whose ancestry is related to Yamnaya-associated groups.

populations.name: Beaker-associated individuals, central and northwest Europe
populations.description: People buried with Bell Beaker material in central and northwest Europe (outside Britain and Iberia), about 2500–2000 BCE, most of whom carry substantial steppe-related ancestry.

populations.name: Beaker-associated individuals, Britain
populations.description: People buried with Bell Beaker material in Britain from about 2450 BCE, with high steppe-related ancestry, unlike Britain's Neolithic population.

populations.name: Chalcolithic people of Iberia (including Beaker-associated individuals)
populations.description: Individuals from Copper Age Iberia (about 3000–2200 BCE), among them many buried with Bell Beaker material. Most resemble earlier Iberian populations and lack steppe-related ancestry, so the same pottery style travelled with different people in different places.
populations.archaeological_context: Iberian Chalcolithic, including Bell Beaker contexts.

membership.notes: AADR v66.p1 labels Iberian Beaker-associated individuals by period (e.g. Spain_C), not by culture, so Beaker association cannot be read from the label. Individuals labelled -oSteppe form a separate population.

caveats: Grouped by region and period because the AADR labels do not record Beaker association.

populations.name: Chalcolithic Iberians with steppe-related ancestry
populations.description: A minority of Copper Age Iberians, labelled as genetic outliers in AADR, who carry steppe-related ancestry. They are the earliest detection of such ancestry in the peninsula.

membership.notes: Uses the AADR outlier label deliberately; the default outlier exclusion is overridden for this population.

caveats: Defined by an AADR outlier label; the exact correspondence to the 8 individuals of Olalde 2018 is not checked individual by individual.

populations.name: Bronze Age people of Iberia
populations.description: Individuals from Bronze Age Iberia (about 2200–900 BCE). By about 2000 BCE a large share of their ancestry, and nearly all Y chromosomes, derive from people with steppe-related ancestry.

membership.notes: Grouped by region and period, not by a single genetic profile.

populations.name: Late Bronze Age and Iron Age people of southern Britain
populations.description: Individuals from England and Wales from the Late Bronze Age onward, whose ancestry shifted towards more early-farmer-related ancestry through migrants from the continent.

populations.name: Middle–Late Bronze Age steppe (Sintashta, Andronovo, Srubnaya-associated)
populations.description: People of the central Eurasian steppe in the 2nd millennium BCE associated with the Sintashta, Petrovka, Alakul/Andronovo and Srubnaya cultures. Ancestry with their profile reached South Asia via Central Asia.

populations.name: Botai-associated individuals
populations.description: People of northern Kazakhstan associated with the Botai culture, linked to the earliest evidence of horse husbandry, whose ancestry derives from hunter-gatherers deeply diverged from the Yamnaya.
caveats: Three individuals.

populations.name: Indus Periphery Cline and the Rakhigarhi individual
populations.description: A genetic profile shared by one individual from an Indus Valley Civilization context (Rakhigarhi) and by outliers buried at sites in Iran and Turkmenistan that were in contact with the IVC: a mixture of ancient-Iranian-related and South Asian hunter-gatherer-related ancestry, with little or no steppe-related ancestry.

region.name: Northwest South Asia and its periphery

membership.notes: AADR v66.p1 does not label the 11 Indus Periphery outliers separately (they sit inside numbered clusters such as Turkmenistan_BA1-1 and Iran_ShahriSokhta_BA2-2); adding them needs the individual list from Narasimhan 2019.

caveats: Only one genome comes from an IVC context; whether it represents the IVC population as a whole is a hypothesis.
Membership is incomplete (see notes).

populations.name: Ancestral Ancient South Asians (AASI, modelled)
populations.description: A modelled ancestry component: the South Asian lineage with no relationship to West Eurasians, split around the time East Asian, Andamanese and Australian ancestors separated. No unmixed individual has been sampled.

membership.notes: Inferred only.

caveats: The time range is a display window, not a dated lifespan.

populations.name: Ancestral South Indians (ASI, modelled)
populations.description: A modelled ancestral population that formed after the decline of the Indus Valley Civilization as Indus Periphery-related people mixed with groups further southeast. It is one of the two main sources of ancestry in present-day South Asians.

membership.notes: Inferred only.

caveats: Display window; formation date is model-based.

populations.name: Ancestral North Indians (ANI, modelled)
populations.description: A modelled ancestral population that formed in the 2nd millennium BCE as Indus Periphery-related people mixed with people carrying steppe-related ancestry arriving via Central Asia.

membership.notes: Inferred only.

caveats: Display window; formation date is model-based.

populations.name: Jōmon-associated hunter-gatherers
populations.description: Hunter-gatherer-fishers of the Japanese archipelago associated with the Jōmon culture, whose ancestry belongs to a deeply splitting East Asian lineage.

membership.notes: Includes Initial to Final Jōmon individuals.

populations.name: Kofun-period individuals (Japan)
populations.description: Individuals from the Kofun period (about 300–700 CE), whose ancestry adds a large East Asian-related component to earlier Jōmon- and Yayoi-period ancestry.
caveats: Three individuals.

populations.name: Amur River basin hunter-gatherers
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of the Amur River basin, whose ancestry stayed remarkably stable over thousands of years.

populations.name: Yellow River basin Neolithic farmers
populations.description: Millet farmers of the middle and lower Yellow River basin in the Neolithic, whose ancestry later contributed widely in East Asia, including to Tibetan groups and Han Chinese.

populations.name: West Liao River basin Neolithic and Bronze Age people
populations.description: Individuals from the West Liao River region of northeast China, whose ancestry shifted over time, towards the Yellow River with intensifying farming and towards the Amur with Bronze Age pastoralism.

membership.notes: Grouped by region; not a single genetic profile.

populations.name: Iron Age people of Taiwan
populations.description: Individuals from Taiwan (about 1300 BCE–800 CE) carrying mostly southern East Asian ancestry, related to that common in present-day speakers of Austronesian languages, with a smaller northern component.

populations.name: Hòabìnhian-associated hunter-gatherers
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of mainland Southeast Asia associated with the Hòabìnhian technocomplex, whose deeply diverged eastern Eurasian ancestry contributed to later Southeast Asians.
caveats: Two individuals; claims verified against the abstract only.

populations.name: Neolithic farmers of mainland Southeast Asia (Man Bac)
populations.description: Early farmers of northern Vietnam, about 4,000 years ago, whose ancestry combines southern East Asian farmer-related and local hunter-gatherer-related components.

populations.name: Xiongnu-period individuals (Mongolia)
populations.description: People of the Eastern Steppe during the time of the Xiongnu polity (about 200 BCE–100 CE), whose ancestry reflects mixing of earlier Mongolian and surrounding populations.
caveats: 'Xiongnu-period' is a date-and-place grouping; it does not imply a single ethnic identity.

populations.name: Mongol-period individuals (Mongolia)
populations.description: People of Mongolia during the Mongol Empire era (about 1200–1400 CE), with much higher eastern Eurasian ancestry than in the Xiongnu period.

membership.notes: AADR uses 'LateMedieval' for the Mongol period.

caveats: A date-and-place grouping, not an ethnic identity.

populations.name: Founding population of Native Americans (inferred)
populations.description: A modelled population: the shared ancestors of Ancient Beringians and all other Native Americans, which separated from East Asian-related populations, received gene flow related to Ancient North Eurasians, and later branched. Its location during this time is not known from genetics.

region.name: Northeast Asia / Beringia (not located by genetics)

membership.notes: Inferred only.

caveats: The window spans the modelled split from East Asians (~36,000 years ago) to the divergence of northern and southern branches (~14,600 years ago, lower bound) in Moreno-Mayar 2018 (abstract only); other studies place the founding migration later (no earlier than 23,000 years ago, Raghavan 2015).

populations.name: Ancient Beringians (Upward Sun River)
populations.description: Two infants buried at Upward Sun River, Alaska, about 11,500 years ago, representing a population basal to all other Native Americans.
caveats: Claims verified against the abstract only.

populations.name: Anzick-1 (Clovis-associated)
populations.description: An infant buried with Clovis tools in Montana about 12,600 years ago, more closely related to all Indigenous Americans than to any other population.
caveats: A single individual.

populations.name: Early Holocene people of Central and South America
populations.description: The oldest sampled individuals from Belize, Brazil, Chile, Peru and Argentina (before about 8,000 years ago). Some of the earliest share an affinity with Anzick-1 that is absent in later South Americans.

membership.notes: Grouped by region and date: these individuals do not form one genetic cluster.

caveats: AADR labels for early Belize individuals contain 'Archaic_Maya', projecting a much later identity back in time; we keep the label as data only.

populations.name: People of the Central and South-Central Andes
populations.description: Individuals from the Andean highlands and Pacific coast of Peru and Bolivia over the last 9,000 years, among whom present-day Andean genetic structure began forming by about 5,800 years ago.

membership.notes: Grouped by region.

populations.name: Archaic Age people of the Caribbean
populations.description: The Caribbean's first inhabitants, before the Ceramic Age, descended from a deeply divergent population closest to Central and northern South Americans.

populations.name: Ceramic Age people of the Caribbean
populations.description: Ceramic-using people of the Caribbean from at least 1,700 years ago, genetically homogeneous and related to Arawak-speaking groups of northeastern South America; their arrival almost entirely replaced Archaic Age ancestry.

populations.name: Ancestors of Papuans and Aboriginal Australians (inferred)
populations.description: A modelled population: the ancestors of present-day Papuans and Aboriginal Australians, who carry more Denisovan-related ancestry than other non-Africans. No ancient genome from this population falls in the V1 window.

region.name: Island Southeast Asia and Sahul (not located by genetics)

membership.notes: Inferred from present-day genomes.

caveats: Display window only: the cited sources do not date this population.

populations.name: First Remote Oceanians (Lapita-associated)
populations.description: The first people to settle Vanuatu and Tonga, about 3,000 years ago, buried with Lapita material. Their ancestry was almost entirely East Asian-related, with little or no Papuan-related ancestry.

populations.name: Post-Lapita people of Vanuatu
populations.description: People of Vanuatu from about 2,300 years ago onward, whose ancestry is predominantly Papuan-related, while Austronesian languages continued to be spoken.

populations.name: Bismarck Archipelago-related ancestry (source, inferred)
populations.description: The source of the Papuan-related ancestry that reached Vanuatu, best matched by present-day people of the Bismarck Archipelago. No ancient individual from the source has been sampled.

membership.notes: Inferred from present-day genomes.

location_hint.label: Bismarck Archipelago (region named in the source)

caveats: Display window spans the arrival of Papuan-related ancestry in Vanuatu, not a lifespan.

populations.name: Mota (Ethiopia)
populations.description: A man who lived about 4,500 years ago in the Ethiopian highlands, whose genome predates the Eurasian-related admixture found in many present-day eastern Africans.
caveats: The source paper carries an erratum; only claims unaffected by it are used.
A single individual.

populations.name: Eastern African foragers
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of eastern Africa over the last 18,000 years, carrying a deep eastern African lineage. Their ancestry later mixed with incoming herders and farmers.
caveats: Few individuals across a very large area and time span.

populations.name: Foragers of Malawi
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of Malawi between about 15,000 and 2,500 years ago, about two-thirds of whose ancestry is related to that of present-day southern African San.

populations.name: Southern African foragers
populations.description: Stone Age hunter-gatherers of southern Africa, genetically similar to present-day southern San groups.

populations.name: Shum Laka individuals (Cameroon)
populations.description: Children buried at the Shum Laka rock shelter in Cameroon about 8,000 and 3,000 years ago, with ancestry most similar to west-central African hunter-gatherers.
caveats: Four individuals.

populations.name: Pastoral Neolithic herders of eastern Africa
populations.description: The first herders of Kenya and Tanzania, about 5,000–1,200 years ago, formed by mixing between northeastern African-related peoples and local foragers. Makers of different Pastoral Neolithic artefact traditions were not genetically distinct.

membership.notes: Tanzania_3000BP is the Luxmanda individual (Skoglund 2017).

populations.name: Iron Age farmers with western-African-related ancestry
populations.description: Iron Age individuals in eastern and southern Africa whose ancestry is mostly related to present-day western African and Bantu-speaking populations. They are associated with the spread of farming and of Bantu languages, which brought complete replacement of local foragers in some regions.
caveats: A linguistic label (Bantu) is used here only to describe an association; the population is defined genetically.

populations.name: Medieval people of the Swahili coast
populations.description: Townspeople of the medieval Swahili coast, from about 1250 CE, with African ancestry inherited mainly through women and Asian (mainly Persian-related) ancestry inherited mainly through men, mixing from about 1000 CE.

membership.notes: Limited to individuals overlapping the V1 window.

relationships.wording: The Zlatý kůň/Ranis population is the earliest sampled branch of the population that left Africa and received Neandertal gene flow.
relationships.time_note: Time not estimated in the cited sources; drawn while both populations are attested.

relationships.wording: Ust'-Ishim derives from the shared non-African population, before or around the separation of western and eastern Eurasians.
relationships.time_note: Time not estimated in the cited sources; drawn while both populations are attested.

relationships.wording: Tianyuan shares extra genetic affinity with Goyet Q116-1, so early European and Asian populations did not separate in one clean split.
relationships.time_note: Time not estimated in the cited sources; drawn across the gap between them.

relationships.wording: Ancestry of the early European founder population (Kostenki/Sunghir-related) contributed to Gravettian-associated groups of central and southern Europe.
relationships.time_note: Time not estimated in the cited sources; drawn across the gap between them.

relationships.wording: Ancient North Siberians were distantly related to early western Eurasian hunter-gatherers.
relationships.time_note: Time not estimated in the cited sources; drawn while both populations are attested.

relationships.wording: Gravettian-associated people of western Europe (Fournol cluster) carried ancestry closely related to that of earlier Aurignacian-associated individuals from Goyet.
relationships.time_note: Time not estimated in the cited sources; drawn across the gap between them.

relationships.wording: Fournol-related ancestry persisted through the Last Glacial Maximum in southwestern Europe.
relationships.time_note: Time not estimated in the cited sources; drawn across the gap between them.

relationships.wording: Fournol-related ancestry continued from Solutrean- to Magdalenian-associated people.
relationships.time_note: Time not estimated in the cited sources; drawn across the gap between them.

relationships.time_basis: from at least 14,000 years ago (Posth 2023); Villabruna cluster from ~14 ka (Fu 2016)
relationships.wording: From at least 14,000 years ago, Villabruna-related ancestry spread from the south across western and central Europe, largely replacing Magdalenian-associated ancestry.

evidence.claim: Neandertals share more derived variants with present-day people outside sub-Saharan Africa than with sub-Saharan Africans, best explained by gene flow from Neandertals into the ancestors of non-Africans before Eurasian populations diverged.
A finger bone from Denisova Cave yielded the genome of an archaic group related to Neandertals, named Denisovans.
Denisovan-related ancestry was first estimated at 4–6% of the genomes of present-day Melanesians.
evidence.location: Abstract; section on Denisovan gene flow into Melanesians
evidence.note: First estimate; later work refines Denisovan proportions.

evidence.claim: Neandertal-derived DNA in people outside Africa was estimated at 1.5–2.1%.
evidence.location: Gene-flow section; SI 14; Extended Data Table 1

evidence.claim: The Neandertal ancestry in non-Africans is closer to the Mezmaiskaya (Caucasus) Neandertal than to the Altai Neandertal.
Gene flow from Neandertals into Denisovans contributed at least about 0.5% of the Denisovan genome.
The Vindija and Mezmaiskaya Neandertals are closer than the Altai Neandertal to the Neandertals who contributed DNA to present-day non-Africans.
Revised estimate: non-Africans outside Oceania carry 1.8–2.6% Neandertal DNA (East Asians 2.3–2.6%, western Eurasians 1.8–2.4%).
Linkage disequilibrium in present-day Europeans dates the last Neandertal gene flow to 37,000–86,000 years ago, most likely 47,000–65,000 years ago.
Ust'-Ishim (~45,000 years old, western Siberia) belonged to a population that lived before or around the separation of western and eastern Eurasians.
Ust'-Ishim's Neandertal segments are longer than in present-day people, placing the Neandertal gene flow about 7,000–13,000 years before he lived.
Site-frequency-spectrum modelling places a primary Neandertal admixture of about 2.3% (95% CI 1.1–3.5%) in the ancestors of all non-Africans at about 60,000 years ago (95% CI 55–84 ka).
Aboriginal Australians and Papuans carry more Denisovan-derived haplotypes than other non-Africans.
evidence.location: Archaic admixture section; Extended Data Fig. 3

evidence.claim: Most Neandertal ancestry in modern humans traces to a single extended period of gene flow 50,500–43,500 years ago, shared by most non-Africans.

Individuals from Ranis (Germany) and Zlatý kůň (Czechia), about 45,000 years old, belong to one small, closely related population that is the earliest split from the out-of-Africa population sampled so far and shows no continuity with later Europeans.
The Neandertal ancestry of the Zlatý kůň/Ranis population comes from the admixture shared by all non-Africans, dated to 45,000–49,000 years ago.

Three individuals from Bacho Kiro Cave (Bulgaria), dated ~45,900–42,600 years ago and associated with an Initial Upper Palaeolithic assemblage, are more closely related to later East Asians and Native Americans than to later western Eurasians, and each had a Neandertal ancestor a few generations back.
Oase 1 (Romania, ~37,000–42,000 years old) has about 6–9% Neandertal DNA, implying a Neandertal ancestor 4–6 generations back, and shows no special relationship to later Europeans.

Denisovan-introgressed segments in present-day Chinese and Japanese populations fall into two components with different affinity to the Altai Denisovan, indicating at least two Denisovan-related sources.
evidence.location: Section 'Two waves of Denisovan ancestry'; Fig. 4; Table 2

evidence.claim: Ayta Magbukon (Philippines) carry about 30–40% more Denisovan ancestry than Australians and Papuans, consistent with a separate Denisovan admixture event.
Neandertal ancestry in European individuals fell from 3–6% in the earliest to about 2% over 45,000–7,000 years ago.

From about 37,000 years ago (Kostenki 14) to about 14,000 years ago, all sampled Europeans descend from one founder population that is part of present-day European ancestry; earlier individuals such as Oase 1 did not contribute substantially.

Genetically defined clusters, named after type sites: Věstonice (Gravettian-associated), Mal'ta, El Mirón (Magdalenian-associated, with affinity to GoyetQ116-1) and Villabruna (from ~14,000 years ago).
From about 14,000 years ago a component related to present-day Near Easterners appears in Europe with the Villabruna cluster.

Hunter-gatherer clusters before and after the LGM: Fournol (Gravettian-associated, western Europe, related to Aurignacian-associated Goyet Q116-1), Věstonice (Gravettian-associated, central and southern Europe), GoyetQ2 (Magdalenian-associated), Villabruna (Epigravettian-associated), Oberkassel (equated with WHG), and Sidelkino (renamed EHG).
Gravettian-associated individuals form two genetically distinct clusters (Fournol in the west, Věstonice in central and southern Europe): one archaeological culture, two genetic profiles.
Fournol-related ancestry persisted through the LGM in southwestern Europe in Solutrean- and then Magdalenian-associated individuals.
From at least 14,000 years ago, Villabruna/Oberkassel-related ancestry spread from the south across Europe, largely replacing Magdalenian-associated (GoyetQ2) ancestry.
Magdalenian-associated individuals are modelled as mixtures of Fournol- and Villabruna-related ancestry; El Mirón carries about 43% Villabruna-related ancestry, others 19–29%.

From about 8,000 years ago, Sidelkino (EHG)-related ancestry appears at about 10% in central European hunter-gatherers, and Oberkassel-related ancestry reaches the upper Volga by at least 7,500 years ago.
Gravettian-associated individuals from Goyet (Belgium) are genetically intermediate between the Věstonice and Fournol clusters, contrary to their earlier assignment by Fu et al. 2016.
Eastern hunter-gatherer (EHG/Sidelkino) ancestry shows affinity to both Villabruna-related and Ancient North Eurasian ancestry.

Most present-day Europeans can be modelled with ancestry from three deeply differentiated sources: West European Hunter-Gatherers (WHG), Ancient North Eurasians (ANE) and Early European Farmers (EEF).
Early European Farmers are modelled with about 44% ancestry from a 'Basal Eurasian' lineage that split before other non-African lineages diversified.
evidence.note: Basal Eurasian is a modelled lineage without sampled individuals.

evidence.claim: Caucasus hunter-gatherers (Satsurblia ~13,300 years ago, Kotias Klde ~9,700 years ago, western Georgia) form a distinct ancient clade.
Model-based split times: CHG from WHG about 45,000 years ago, and from the ancestors of Neolithic farmers about 25,000 years ago.
CHG-related ancestry contributed significantly to Yamnaya-associated steppe herders.

MA-1 (Mal'ta, south-central Siberia, ~24,000 years ago) is basal to present-day western Eurasians and related to Native Americans, without close affinity to East Asians; Afontova Gora 2 (~17,000 years ago) shows similar ancestry.
An estimated 14–38% of Native American ancestry may derive from gene flow from a population related to MA-1, after divergence from East Asian ancestors and before Native American diversification.

Northeastern Siberia saw an initial Palaeolithic 'Ancient North Siberian' population (Yana, ~31,000 years ago) distantly related to early West Eurasian hunter-gatherers, then East Asian-related people who gave rise to Native Americans and 'Ancient Paleosiberians', then Holocene 'Neosiberians'; each expansion nearly replaced earlier inhabitants.

Seven ~15,000-year-old Iberomaurusian-associated individuals from Taforalt (Morocco) show affinity with Natufians, no gene flow from Palaeolithic Europeans, and about one-third sub-Saharan African-related ancestry.

Tianyuan (~40,000 years old, China) is more related to Asians than to Europeans but shares extra alleles with Goyet Q116-1 (~35,000 years old, Belgium), so early European and Asian populations did not separate in one clean split.
The earliest sampled Near Eastern populations derived about half their ancestry from a 'Basal Eurasian' lineage with little or no Neandertal ancestry.
The first farmers of the southern Levant and of the Zagros were strongly differentiated, each descending largely from local hunter-gatherers.
By the Bronze Age, Levant-, Zagros- and Anatolia-related farmer ancestries had mixed, reducing genetic differentiation across the Near East.
Farmer ancestry related to Anatolian farmers spread west into Europe.
East African ancestry is better modelled by Levantine early farmers than by Anatolian or European farmers: Levant-related farmer ancestry contributed to East Africa.
Ancestry related to Iranian farmers spread north into the Eurasian steppe.
People related to both early Iranian farmers and steppe pastoralists spread east into South Asia.
evidence.note: The Iranian-farmer part is contested by Shinde 2019 and Narasimhan 2019.

evidence.claim: Early Neolithic people of the Zagros were neither ancestral to the first European farmers nor significant contributors to present-day Europeans; multiple differentiated hunter-gatherer populations adopted farming in southwest Asia.
Model-based separation of Zagros and Anatolian early farmers' ancestors: about 46,000–77,000 years ago.

Central Anatolian early farmers show about 80–90% genetic continuity with a ~15,000-year-old local hunter-gatherer (Pınarbaşı), with additional Iranian/Caucasus-related and later Levant-related ancestry.
Late Chalcolithic individuals from Peqi'in Cave (Israel, 4500–3900 BCE) are modelled as about 57% Levant Neolithic-related, 17% Iran Chalcolithic-related and 26% Anatolia Neolithic-related.
Farming reached southeastern Europe in the mid-7th millennium BCE with migrants of Anatolian-related ancestry.
European hunter-gatherers formed a west–east cline of ancestry.
The first farmers of northern and western Europe passed through southeastern Europe with limited hunter-gatherer admixture; some groups that remained there mixed extensively.
Hunter-gatherer ancestry in early European farmers varied by region and generally increased over time through local admixture.
Hunter-gatherer ancestry estimates: LBK about 4–5% (admixture dated 5545 ± 65 BCE); German Middle Neolithic about 17%; Iberian Middle Neolithic about 23%; Iberian Chalcolithic about 27%.

Farming came to Britain with continental farmers whose ancestry was mostly Anatolian-farmer-related (about 74% on average in the authors' model), with small hunter-gatherer contributions and no later hunter-gatherer resurgence.
British Neolithic individuals show affinities with Iberian Neolithic individuals, suggesting descent mainly from farmers who followed the Mediterranean route.
Continental farmers are modelled as arriving in Britain by 3975–3722 cal BCE (95%).

8,000–7,000 years ago, early farmers in Germany, Hungary and Spain were closely related to each other and distinct from local hunter-gatherers, while Russia was inhabited by hunter-gatherers (EHG) with high affinity to the 24,000-year-old Mal'ta individual.
Middle Neolithic populations of Germany and Spain carry about 18–34% more WHG-related ancestry than Early Neolithic populations.
Yamnaya-associated steppe herders descended from eastern European hunter-gatherers and from a population of Near Eastern ancestry.
Corded Ware-associated individuals from Germany derive about 75% of their ancestry from a Yamnaya-related source; modelled against Middle Neolithic populations, the turnover is 48–80%.
Steppe-related ancestry persisted in all sampled central Europeans to at least 3,000 years ago; Bell Beaker- and Únětice-associated groups carry less of it than Corded Ware-associated individuals.
Iberian and central European Beaker-associated individuals had limited genetic affinity, so the Beaker complex spread between these regions mainly through cultural transmission.
Steppe-related ancestry is present in most Beaker-associated individuals outside Iberia, but in only 8 of 32 Iberian Beaker-associated individuals.
In Britain, the arrival of the Beaker complex brought high steppe-related ancestry and was associated with replacement of about 90% of the gene pool within a few hundred years.
Iberian hunter-gatherers showed strong substructure between the northwest and southeast before farming.
By about 2000 BCE, about 40% of Iberia's ancestry and nearly 100% of its Y chromosomes derive from people with steppe-related ancestry: a strongly male-biased process.
A genetic boundary from the Black Sea to the Baltic separated differentiated hunter-gatherers; farming brought large ancestry shifts west of it and none of substance east of it in the same period.
Yamnaya-related ancestry spread across western Eurasia from about 5,000 years ago, reaching most of Europe within about 1,000 years.
Middle Don hunter-gatherers contributed ancestry to Yamnaya-associated groups, which later admixed with Globular Amphora-associated people before expanding into Europe.
Gene flow carried Caucasus- and Anatolian/Levantine-related ancestry north to the steppe; Yamnaya-associated people later spread into the Balkans and across the Caucasus into Armenia.
Bronze Age Anatolia was shaped by gene flow within West Asia, with negligible impact from Yamnaya-related migrations.

The Yamnaya archaeological complex appeared about 3300 BCE north of the Black and Caspian Seas and by 3000 BCE extended from Hungary to Kazakhstan; its individuals are genetically very similar across this range.

Eneolithic people north of the Caucasus form three clines: Caucasus–Lower Volga (CLV, rich in CHG-related ancestry), Volga (CLV mixed with EHG, e.g. Khvalynsk), and Dnipro (CLV mixed with Ukraine Neolithic hunter-gatherers, e.g. Serednii Stih).
Yamnaya ancestors formed about 4000 BCE from Serednii Stih-related groups and grew rapidly after 3750–3350 BCE; CLV-related people contributed about four-fifths of Yamnaya ancestry.
Don Yamnaya are modelled as 79.4 ± 1.1% 'Core Yamnaya' and 20.6 ± 1.1% Ukraine Neolithic hunter-gatherer-related ancestry (qpAdm).
Usatove-associated people formed as CLV-related migrants mixed in roughly equal parts with Trypillia-associated farmers.
A genetically Yamnaya-like individual from Mykhailivka (3635–3383 BCE) bridges Serednii Stih and Yamnaya.
Groups of the Caucasus mountains were genetically separated from contemporaneous steppe groups; Yamnaya and later steppe pastoralists carry farmer-related ancestry from different contact zones.
Botai-associated people, linked to the earliest horse husbandry, derive from hunter-gatherers deeply diverged from the Yamnaya.
No steppe-related ancestry was found in Bronze Age Anatolia, and Early Bronze Age Yamnaya-related migrations had limited direct genetic impact in Asia compared with Europe.

Between 1000 and 875 BCE, EEF-related ancestry increased in southern Britain through migrants genetically most similar to ancient individuals from France, who contributed about half the ancestry of Iron Age people of England and Wales.
The main source of ancestry in South Asians is a prehistoric gradient between people related to early Iranian hunter-gatherers and people related to South/Southeast Asian hunter-gatherers (AASI).
Eleven outlier individuals at Gonur and Shahr-i-Sokhta form an 'Indus Periphery Cline'; equating it with the Indus Valley Civilization population is a hypothesis with circumstantial support.

After the IVC's decline, Indus Periphery-related people mixed with south-eastern groups to form Ancestral South Indians (ASI), and with steppe-pastoralist-descended people arriving via Central Asia after ~4000 years ago to form Ancestral North Indians (ANI).
AASI ('Ancestral Ancient South Asians') is modelled as an Asian lineage that split around the time East Asian, Andamanese and Australian ancestors separated.
Steppe-related ancestry in South Asia has the same profile as that of Bronze Age eastern Europe.

A genome from an IVC context (Rakhigarhi) fits as a mixture of ancient-Iranian-related (largest) and Southeast Asian hunter-gatherer-related ancestry, matching the Indus Periphery outliers, with little or no steppe-related ancestry.

The Iranian-related ancestry in the IVC individual derives from a lineage that split before the ancestors of early Iranian farmers, herders and hunter-gatherers separated, contradicting a large-scale eastward spread of western Iranian farmers.
Jōmon-associated hunter-gatherers, Amur Basin hunter-gatherers, and Neolithic/Iron Age Taiwan and Tibetan-plateau people share a deeply splitting lineage.
evidence.note: The authors' interpretation as a Late Pleistocene coastal migration is not displayed as a route.

evidence.claim: Yellow River farmer-related ancestry (around 3000 BCE) contributed up to about 84% to some Tibetan groups and about 59–84% to Han Chinese.

Individuals from Taiwan (~1300 BCE–800 CE) derive about 75% of their ancestry from a southern lineage (likely Yangtze-farmer-related) and about 25% from a northern lineage related to but distinct from Yellow River farmers.
Yamnaya-related steppe ancestry reached western Mongolia after about 3000 BCE.

Amur River populations were genetically stable from 7500 to 1700 BP, while Yellow River and West Liao River profiles changed; Yellow River populations grew increasingly similar to present-day southern Chinese and Southeast Asians over time.
In the West Liao River region, Late Neolithic farming intensification coincides with increased Yellow River affinity, and Bronze Age pastoralism with increased Amur affinity.
Northern East Asian ancestry spread across southern East Asia after the Neolithic; Neolithic southern East Asian and Taiwan Strait individuals show Austronesian-related connections.

Early farmers at Man Bac (Vietnam) mix East Asian (southern-Chinese-agriculturalist-related) and deeply diverged eastern Eurasian hunter-gatherer ancestry; by the Bronze Age, sites in Vietnam and Myanmar show further influxes.
Both Hòabìnhian hunter-gatherer-related and East Asian farmer-related ancestry contributed to Southeast Asian diversity.
Japanese archipelago: Jōmon-related ancestry, then Northeast Asian-related ancestry in the Yayoi period, then East Asian-related ancestry in the Kofun period.
A ~2,500-year-old Jōmon-context individual (IK002) forms a lineage basal to the East and Northeast Asian genomes examined.
A pastoralist expansion reached Mongolia around 3000 BCE; by the Late Bronze Age three genetically structured groups all practised dairy pastoralism regardless of ancestry.
Xiongnu-period individuals formed from mixture of earlier Mongolian and surrounding populations; Mongol-period individuals show much higher eastern Eurasian ancestry.
Anzick-1, an infant buried with Clovis tools in Montana (~12,700–12,550 cal BP), is more closely related to all Indigenous American populations than to any other group.
The ANE (Mal'ta)-related gene flow into Native American ancestors is shared by Anzick-1, so it happened before about 12,600 years ago.
The ancestors of all present-day Native Americans entered the Americas from Siberia as a single migration wave no earlier than 23,000 years ago, after at most ~8,000 years of isolation in Beringia.
Native Americans diversified into two basal branches around 13,000 years ago.

Later gene flow led some Native Americans to share ancestry with present-day East Asians and, more distantly, with Australo-Melanesians; putative 'Paleoamerican' relict groups are not directly related to Australo-Melanesians.
USR1 (Upward Sun River, Alaska, ~11,500 years ago) is basal to all other Native Americans and represents a distinct Ancient Beringian population.

Demographic model: split from East Asians ~36 ± 1.5 ka with gene flow until ~25 ka; ANE-related gene flow 25–20 ka; Ancient Beringians branched 22–18.1 ka; northern and southern Native American branches diverged 17.5–14.6 ka.
Some Amazonian groups carry ancestry from a founding source ('Population Y') with extra affinity to Australasians, not seen in Anzick-1 or North and Central Americans.
evidence.note: Signal from present-day genomes; source population unsampled.

evidence.claim: Rapid early dispersal and diversification within the Americas, including one migration with an Australasian-related signal and a later Mesoamerican-related expansion.
Central and South Americans radiated rapidly from one of the two early Native American branches.
Two streams of North–South gene flow: one reaching the Central Andes by about 4,200 years ago, and one linking Anzick-1 to the oldest individuals from Chile, Brazil and Belize.
Later South Americans derive from lineages without specific Clovis affinity: a population replacement beginning at least 9,000 years ago, followed by substantial regional continuity.

Present-day Andean genetic structure began to form by about 5,800 years ago; neighbouring Andean groups show minimal admixture 2,000–500 years ago, with mixed-ancestry communities in the Tiwanaku and Inca heartlands.
Archaic Age Caribbean people derive from a deeply divergent population closest to Central and northern South Americans.

Archaic Caribbean lineages were more than 98% replaced by a homogeneous ceramic-using population related to Arawak speakers of northeastern South America, which reached the Greater Antilles at least 1,700 years ago.
Changes in pottery style within the Ceramic Age were not driven by migration of genetically distinct groups.
Human footprints at White Sands (New Mexico) are bracketed by seed layers with calibrated radiocarbon ages of about 23,000–21,000 years ago.
evidence.note: Archaeological evidence; dating debated in later literature not yet reviewed here.

evidence.claim: Lapita-associated individuals from Vanuatu (~3,100–2,700 years ago) and Tonga (~2,700–2,300 years ago) had little or no Papuan-related ancestry.
Present-day South Pacific populations carry at least 25% Papuan-related ancestry, which must have spread after first settlement.
The first Remote Oceanians descend directly from the population that spread from Taiwan via the Philippines to western Melanesia from about 5,000 years ago, with minimal admixture along the way.
People of almost entirely Papuan-related ancestry reached Vanuatu by about 2,300 years ago; Papuan-related ancestry was later diluted but remains at least 80–90% on most islands.
The Papuan-related ancestry in Vanuatu derives from the Bismarck Archipelago.

A Papuan-related expansion into Remote Oceania began about 2,500 years ago and led to near-complete replacement of Lapita-related ancestry in Vanuatu through repeated migrations and sex-biased admixture, while Austronesian languages persisted.

Present-day genomes suggest a serial-founder settlement of Polynesia from Samoa through Rarotonga to the Society Islands (~11th century), Austral and Tuāmotu (~12th century), and Marquesas, Raivavae and Rapa Nui (~1200 CE).

San-related ancestry was once more widespread: about two-thirds of the ancestry of Malawi hunter-gatherers (~8,100–2,500 years ago) and about one-third of Tanzanian hunter-gatherers (~1,400 years ago).
The spread of farmers from western Africa involved complete replacement of local hunter-gatherers in some regions.

A ~3,100-year-old pastoralist from Luxmanda (Tanzania) is modelled with 38 ± 1% ancestry related to Levantine pre-pottery farmers (Iran- or Anatolia-related sources excluded); the authors note this could reflect migration from the Levant or a shared earlier ancestral population.

Children buried at Shum Laka (Cameroon) ~8,000 and ~3,000 years ago have ancestry most similar to west-central African hunter-gatherers; present-day Bantu speakers do not descend substantially from this population.
Eastern and south-central African forager ancestry is a geographically structured mixture of three highly divergent sources, probably formed 80,000–20,000 years ago and stable afterwards.

East African pastoralist groups formed through admixture between northeastern-African-related peoples and eastern African foragers, with further northeastern- and western-African-related admixture by the Iron Age.
Makers of distinct Pastoral Neolithic artefact traditions were not genetically differentiated.
Kenyan pastoralist individuals carry variable Dinka-related and eastern-forager-related ancestry (e.g. 33 ± 11% Dinka-related at Hyrax Hill, ~2,300 years ago).
Genetic diversity among Bantu-speaking populations declines with distance from western Africa, supporting a serial-founder expansion, with significant gene flow from local groups.
~2,000-year-old Stone Age individuals from KwaZulu-Natal resemble present-day southern San; Iron Age individuals (300–500 years old) resemble present-day Bantu-language speakers.

Many medieval Swahili coast individuals derive more than half their DNA from African ancestors (mainly female-line) and much of the rest from Asian ancestors, 80–90% of whose DNA traces to Persian-related men; mixing began by about 1000 CE.

After a 2016 erratum, Mota (Ethiopia, ~4,500 years old) is retained as a high-coverage eastern African genome predating Eurasian-related admixture in eastern Africa; the original claim of Eurasian ancestry in Yoruba and Mbuti was withdrawn.

disagreements.topic: When did the main Neandertal admixture happen?
disagreements.summary: Estimates range from 37,000–86,000 years ago (linkage disequilibrium in present-day genomes) to 45,000–49,000 years ago (anchored by a ~45,000-year-old genome). Recent estimates that use early ancient genomes cluster around 50,000–45,000 years ago.

disagreements.topic: How much Neandertal ancestry do non-Africans carry?
disagreements.summary: Estimates differ with the reference Neandertal genome and method: 1.5–2.1% with the Altai genome, 1.8–2.6% with the closer Vindija genome, about 2.3% in a demographic model.

All models combine southern (Caucasus/Near Eastern-related) and northern (eastern European hunter-gatherer-related) ancestry, but they differ in the sources and routes: EHG plus a Near Eastern-related population; a large CHG-related or Iranian farmer-related contribution; a contribution from Middle Don hunter-gatherers; or about four-fifths Caucasus–Lower Volga-related ancestry plus Ukraine Neolithic hunter-gatherer-related ancestry via Serednii Stih-related groups.

disagreements.topic: Did early Iranian farmers spread east into South Asia?
disagreements.summary: One study describes ancestry related to early Iranian farmers spreading east into South Asia. Later work with an Indus Valley Civilization genome finds that the Iranian-related ancestry in the Indus Periphery split before the lineage of Zagros farmers, which argues against a spread of western Iranian farmers.

positions.label: earlier-splitting Iranian-related lineage; no farmer spread

disagreements.topic: Which cluster do the Goyet Gravettian individuals belong to?
disagreements.summary: Fu et al. 2016 grouped Gravettian-associated individuals from Goyet with the Věstonice cluster; Posth et al. 2023 find them genetically intermediate between the Věstonice and Fournol clusters. They are left unassigned here.

disagreements.topic: When did people first enter the Americas?
disagreements.summary: Genetic models differ: a single founding wave no earlier than 23,000 years ago, or a founding population that split from East Asians about 36,000 years ago with a long period of structure in Beringia. Footprints at White Sands dated about 23,000–21,000 years ago place people in North America during the Last Glacial Maximum; their dating has been debated.

positions.label: founding wave no earlier than 23 ka
split from East Asians ~36 ka; Beringian structure

disagreements.topic: Where does the Australasian-related signal in some Native Americans come from?
disagreements.summary: One study attributes it to an additional founding population ('Population Y'); another attributes distant Australo-Melanesian sharing to later gene flow. The source population is unsampled.

disagreements.topic: How did Levant-related ancestry reach eastern African herders?
disagreements.summary: The Levant-related ancestry of early eastern African herders could reflect migration from the Levant or a shared ancestral population that lived earlier in Africa or the Near East; the study that reports it offers both explanations.

disagreements.topic: How did Papuan-related ancestry arrive in Vanuatu?
disagreements.summary: Studies agree that Papuan-related ancestry arrived soon after first settlement and came to dominate. They differ in timing (by ~2,300 vs from ~2,500 years ago) and in emphasis: one large movement, or repeated, incremental, sex-biased admixture.
